Females of Argentine hake (Merluccius hubbsi) attain sexual maturity at a total length of 31.9 cm [Lp = 31.9 cm], a value derived from extensive field sampling of ovarian condition along the Patagonian shelf. This length at puberty is associated with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 210 grams [Wwp = 210 grams], a substantial somatic investment that reflects the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning. The transition to reproductive competence occurs relatively early in the species' overall growth trajectory, given that the ultimate total length recorded for this population reaches 95 cm [Li = 95 cm], with the maximum adult body mass approaching 5900 grams [Wwi = 5900 grams]. These asymptotic dimensions, observed in the oldest and largest individuals from commercial catch data, underscore the considerable scope for continued somatic expansion after the onset of maturity. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a peak value of 25% [GSI = 25%] under the stable bottom temperatures typical of the spawning grounds at 7 °C [T = 7 °C].

Embryonic development in Merluccius hubbsi is strongly modulated by ambient thermal conditions, with the interval from fertilisation to hatching showing a predictable inverse relationship with temperature. At the relatively cool temperatures characteristic of the species' deep-water nursery areas, recorded at 9.1 °C [T = 9.1 °C], the age at birth is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], a duration that aligns well with the developmental rates reported for other Merlucciidae at comparable thermal regimes. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an initial wet weight at birth of 0.00034 grams [Wwb = 0.00034 grams], a mass that corresponds to the dry weight of the pre-hatching egg, estimated from a mean egg diameter of 866 micrometers. This modest endowment of endogenous yolk must sustain the endotrophic larva through the mouth-opening and first-feeding stages, during which the developing retina and mouth gape achieve functional competence. The rapid depletion of these limited reserves imposes a narrow window for successful transition to exogenous feeding, a critical bottleneck that is likely exacerbated by interannual variability in the timing of the spring phytoplankton bloom, which governs the availability of suitable zooplankton prey for the exogenously feeding larva.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of the Patagonian shelf, where bottom temperatures hover near 7 °C [T = 7 °C] throughout much of the year, the maximum lifespan recorded for Argentine hake reaches approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days], corresponding to an estimated longevity of around twenty years in the oldest individuals. This comparatively extended lifespan, notable among demersal gadiform fishes of the South Atlantic, is accompanied by a relatively slow pace of life, particularly in the early developmental stages. Female juveniles, for instance, do not achieve reproductive maturity until approximately 730 days after hatching [tp = approximately 730 days after hatching], a protracted interval that reflects the time required to reach the critical length of 31.9 cm [Lp = 31.9 cm] at which pubert at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]y is initiated. This extended pre-reproductive period is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy that buffers recruitment against the high interannual variability in larval survival associated with fluctuating prey availability and advective losses from the nursery grounds. The combination of delayed maturity and a long adult lifespan positions this species as a relatively K-selected member of the merlucciid lineage.

 The peak gonadosomatic index of 25% [GSI = 25%] was recorded under the stable thermal conditions at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] during the main spawning pulse in late winter. This high reproductive investment is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy in which multiple egg batches are hydrated and released over several weeks, increasing the likelihood that at least some cohorts encounter favourable feeding conditions for the exogenously feeding larva. The eggs themselves, with a mean diameter of 866 micrometers, are relatively large for a gadiform species, a trait that is associated with the production of a comparatively well-provisioned yolk-sac larva. The initial wet weight at birth of 0.00034 grams [Wwb = 0.00034 grams] is a direct consequence of this egg size, and the resulting larval endowment may confer a survival advantage during the critical period of first feeding, when the timing of prey availability is often unpredictable in the turbulent waters of the Patagonian shelf.

Comparative analysis of body size metrics across the genus Merluccius reveals that Argentine hake occupies an intermediate position in terms of both ultimate total length and ultimate wet weight. With a maximum recorded length of 95 cm [Li = 95 cm] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 5900 grams [Wwi = 5900 grams], the species is considerably smaller than the giant of the genus, Merluccius merluccius, which can exceed 1.4 meters, but is notably larger than several of the eastern Pacific congeners. The length at puberty for females at 31.9 cm [Lp = 31.9 cm] represents approximately 34 percent of the ultimate total length, a ratio that is broadly consistent with the maturation schedule observed in other long-lived demersal fishes. The wet weight at puberty of 210 grams [Wwp = 210 grams] implies that females must increase their body mass by a factor of more than 28 from the age at birth (10 days) [ab = 10 days] to the initiation of spawning, a period of rapid somatic growth that is sustained by the high productivity of the Patagonian shelf ecosystem. The life span of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] places this species among the longer-lived members of its genus, a life-history trait that may buffer the population against recruitment failures and that underscores the importance of maintaining age-structured spawning stock biomass in fisheries management.
